prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, in which magic-wavelength trapping of many atoms brought atomic timekeeping to the 10^-18 level and opened new precision tests of fundamental physics

statement.case_for: After the full first-round exchange I keep optical lattice clocks as my single preferred part, and I can now say why on evidence rather than on the number of supporters. The step that matters is the magic-wavelength lattice: it removes Doppler and recoil shifts to first order while thousands of atoms are interrogated at once, which is what turned an optical clock from a single-ion accuracy device into one with both accuracy and stability at the 1e-18 level. That performance has been reproduced and the clocks compared across independent laboratories (RIKEN/Tokyo, JILA, NIST, PTB, SYRTE, NPL), and the same instruments have measured the gravitational redshift over millimetres and set limits on variation of constants. These are measurements, not projections. The chair asked what wording isolates the lattice advance from the 2005 and 2012 prizes. My answer is that the citation should name the magic-wavelength lattice and the many-atom 10^-18 realisation explicitly, and should not mention combs, ion clocks or the redefinition of the second. The combs gave the means of counting optical cycles and the ion-clock prize honoured quantum control of single ions; neither contains the idea of trapping a large ensemble in a state-insensitive lattice. The credit is Katori for the concept and first demonstrations and Ye for taking the accuracy, stability and many-body clock work to the frontier. No member has proposed a different pair, and the priority checks raised by Lindroth, Olsson and Pearce are about adjacent contributors (Lemonde, Ludlow, Hall, Peik, Hollberg), not about these two. My view on the SI second: the redefinition will follow the evidence and is not a condition for it, so I do not treat timing as a reason to defer.
statement.case_against: The reservation I take most seriously is Olsson's: that this is a third prize in one measurement line, after the 2005 and 2012 prizes, and that Ye would be a repeat laureate. I do not think it is decisive, but I also do not think it can be waved away. If the committee sees the clocks as an engineering path to a better number, the objection wins; if it sees the magic-wavelength lattice as a new capability with its own physics consequences, it does not. I hold the second view because the lattice clock brought a many-body regime (collective interrogation, density shifts, spin-polarised fermions) that single-ion clocks never had. Danielsson's point is also fair, that tests of fundamental physics with these clocks have so far returned null results, so the discovery content is the capability and the redshift measurement, not a detected new effect. Finally, I have not seen an expert report on the Sr-lattice priority history, and if one showed a third name with a claim of the same weight as Katori's or Ye's, I would reopen the credit instead of defending it.

responses.point: Olsson accepts the science and the replication but argues that the lattice clock would be the third prize in one precision-metrology line (combs 2005, ion clocks 2012), that Ye's work builds on comb technology, and that broad opening support does not settle the question.
responses.response: I agree that support counts settle nothing and I do not rest on them. On originality, I would separate what the earlier prizes honoured from what this one does. The comb prize covered the counting of optical cycles and the 2012 prize covered quantum control of single trapped ions. The lattice clock is the realisation that you can hold a large ensemble in a light field that does not shift the clock transition, and that is a different experimental idea with a different error budget. Ye's use of comb technology is an enabling tool, as lasers are for all of us in atomic physics, and not a reason to treat his lattice-clock work as already credited. I also share your wish for confirmed priority on the strontium lattice history, and I agree it should be checked before the citation is final. Where I differ is that I would not let that check, or the repeat-laureate question, decide the matter against a result of this quality.

responses.point: Mehlig prefers topological insulators (Kane, Mele, Molenkamp) for a clean Z2 mechanism and a decisive HgTe experiment, and raised the pending redefinition of the second as a reason to wait on the clocks.
responses.response: On the redefinition we still disagree, and I would ask the committee not to wait for it: the redefinition is a decision that metrologists will take because the clocks already perform, so the result does not depend on it. On your own candidate, I think the HgTe experiment is the kind of decisive demonstration I admire and it is mature. The difficulty I see is the credit rather than the science. Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang proposed the specific HgTe structure that Molenkamp measured, and any triple from Kane, Mele, Molenkamp and Hasan leaves out someone with a claim of equal weight. A citation limited to the quantum spin Hall effect would at least be honest about that, but it still omits the proposers of the experiment. I would move B013 ahead of B053 if an expert report showed a triple that the community would accept; I do not see one yet, whereas the clock pair is not contested by anyone in this committee.

responses.point: Danielsson prefers the experimental Higgs discovery (Gianotti, Della Negra, Virdee) as the most securely confirmed and central result on the list, while admitting that the attribution among four founders is the hardest on the shortlist and listing the clocks as a fallback.
responses.response: I respect the argument that the Higgs observation is the most central result on the list and that the experimental side has waited. My difficulty is not with the science but with the credit for two collaborations of thousands: you name three people, Johansson names a different three and Pearce a third, and I cannot judge from the experimental record which of Gianotti, Della Negra, Jenni and Virdee is the one to leave out. You say yourself that a cleanly attributable prize would then be preferable. I agree and take this as support for sequencing, not as a verdict against B046. I have moved it to my second alternative, and if an expert report on the ATLAS and CMS founding roles produced a defensible trio I would reconsider. On your question about what has been learned about nature from the clocks, I accept that the constant-variation searches are null results so far, but the millimetre-scale redshift measurement is a positive result that exists only because of the lattice clock.

responses.point: Lindroth supports B053 with the same pair and emphasises that the reason is new tests of physics and not a better number, while noting that the Sr-lattice priority history and the credit to contributors such as Lemonde and Ludlow should be checked by an expert report.
responses.response: I agree with you on the reason and I think your framing is the correct one for the citation: it should say what the lattice made possible, not that it is overdue. I accept your correction of my word 'overdue' from round 1. On the expert report, I would ask for three specific checks: the date and content of Katori's magic-wavelength proposal; the first lattice-clock demonstrations from Tokyo, JILA and SYRTE; and whether Lemonde's and Ludlow's contributions are of a kind that the statutes could credit alongside these two. As a fellow atomic physicist I expect the answer to leave the pair unchanged, but expecting it is not the same as having confirmed it.

responses.point: Johansson moved the clock above circuit QED, recommended recusal on B001, and argued that the Katori concept paper is as decisive as the demonstrations, so two names are enough.
responses.response: I accept your point on the concept paper, and I think it is a better reading than my 'measurement over proposals'. In the clock case the proposal fixed the idea and the experiments confirmed it, and the credit should say both. On circuit QED, your recusal on B001 is the sensible course and I will be cautious there too, given my WACQT role. I would add that the recusal makes it difficult for the committee to use B001 as a fallback, so I have replaced it among my alternatives with B016.

uncertainties: Whether the expert reports on the Sr-lattice history confirm Katori and Ye as the right and sufficient pair, or show that a third contributor has a claim of comparable weight.
Whether the committee regards the 2005 and 2012 prizes as leaving room for a third precision-metrology prize; I judge that they do, but I cannot show that it is the only reasonable judgment.
How firm the fundamental-physics results from the clocks are, given that constant-variation and dark-matter searches have so far given null results.
I am less able to judge the attribution questions in particle physics and condensed matter from my own experience and rely on the expert reports and on colleagues there.
statement.conflict_note: I spent a year during my PhD in John Hall's laboratory in Boulder (JILA), the institution where Jun Ye works. This is a scientific lineage tie only; I have not collaborated with Katori or Ye on the clock work, and I regard it as not requiring recusal, but I disclose it for the record on B053. I am part of the WACQT leadership, which overlaps institutionally with Chalmers (Johansson), and I would be cautious on B001 for that reason. I have no stated conflict on B016, B046 or the other listed alternatives.
